World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Farmers probe sheep for magic numbers to navigate drought
World.content:
Diana Tait feels a sheep's spine under its wool, to see if the muscle is dipping, flat or bulging.

She knows it is about a "three" but continues to probe the short ribs with her fingertips to be more exact, to calculate a decimal point, landing on about "3.25".

Diana Tait feels the sheep's back to find its condition score. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

The nurse-turned-sheep-farmer from Dunrobin is learning how to "condition score" sheep along with a group of half a dozen other primary producers on a property near Balmoral in Victoria's west.

Now she knows the technique, her trainer Steve Cotton encourages her to speed up and move through the other sheep in the race, so she can quickly "score" a flock, to figure out whether they have been eating the right amount of food.

A farmer can tell what a sheep's condition is by feeling certain muscles on its back. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

"Don't over complicate it. The more you overthink it, the more you start second-guessing yourself. So as long as you're consistent," he says.

" We're just checking the [sheep's] fuel gauge. "

Later they go into a paddock and Mr Cotton uses shears to cut a small section of dry pasture to weigh and estimate the amount of feed in the entire fenced-off area.

The farming consultant and researcher wants them one day to be able to look at the ground at various points in the paddock to estimate the feed on offer.

Sheep farmers learn how to calculate how much pasture is in their paddocks. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

This is one of many farm visits throughout the year which form part of the Lifetime Ewe Management course, which has been completed by more than 5,000 farmers across the country.

The training program is touted by those who run it as a major industry success at a time when climate change and high input costs, most recently from the war in the Middle East, are putting farmers under pressure to make smart business decisions to stay productive.

Farmers who do the course learn to use an app to monitor their flock and calculate feed. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

Farmers who condition score this sheep know it is a "3.5". (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

Ms Tait built her career in health care, but now, she farms in a part of Victoria that's been hit hard by a recent record-breaking drought, and is predicted to be drier with more extreme weather in the future.

The course has inspired her to improve the way she manages the sheep on her farm, to ensure she makes a healthy income selling them for meat.

She says the course has illustrated the importance of keeping sheep in good condition, or to "maintain their weight", rather than let them "slip away", a major challenge for farmers during a dry spell when the cost of bringing in additional feed is high.

" At the end of the day the aim of farming is to make money and if you're not making the right decisions then you're not going to be making a profit. "

Diana Tait writes notes about sheep nutrition. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

Farmers gather in a woolshed to learn more about the theory of sheep health and pasture management. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

Mr Cotton says the course gives farmers a data-driven framework to follow and helps them especially in tough times.

The trainer wants his students to be able to precisely calculate feed budgets and know how it directly affects the health of a sheep at its various life stages.

"You can sit in a university lecture, as I did for 10 years, and you can get all the science and all the information, but unless you can put that into something practical and implement that on farm, it really means nothing," he says.

" That's where Lifetime Ewe, I think, has been really successful. "

Course brings science into sheep farming

The course is run by Australian Wool Innovation (AWI) and Rural Industries Skill Training Centre (RIST), an agricultural college based near Hamilton in south-west Victoria, a renowned sheep farming hub.

RIST says farmers who have completed the Lifetime Ewe have boosted both lambing rates and the number of sheep their farm can support by about 10 per cent.

RIST chief executive Bill Hamill was leading the agricultural college two decades ago when researchers were developing the course on the same site.

Bill Hamill says the course is backed by extensive research. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

He says at the time a big issue for farmers was merino sheep put so much energy into producing wool that in tough seasons they failed to birth one lamb, let alone the ideal two or "twins".

The "game changer" researchers came up with was a system for farmers to accurately measure the health of their sheep and the food available in their paddocks so they were not wasting resources.

Mr Hamill says it was a more scientific approach compared to how farmers previously observed their animals and pastures.

" You'd drive through the paddock and you'd look at your ewes. But it was not actually getting the data they [farmers] needed. "

Sheep being yarded into a race before they are condition scored. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

Course guides farmer through drought

About a 30-minute drive from Hamilton, at Branxholme, Scott Mullins watches his sheep eat from an automatic feeder and he has calculated exactly what nutrition they need so they are ready for market.

"It is an obsession. We love knowing what they need and then matching that with what we can give them," he says.

Scott Mullins watches sheep in a feedlot on one of the properties he manages. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

He did the Lifetime Ewe course a decade ago and says it was a "light-bulb moment" that made him a much better farmer, so he makes sure his workers do it as well.

The farm manager says what he learned in the course has guided him through the drought, so he could take advantage of high lamb prices.

Scott Mullins uses this spreadsheet to measure what food he needs to give to his sheep at their various life stages. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

"The drought was stressful, some of the hardest times of my career, [but] we did actually come through it reasonably confidently," he says.

"I didn't have surprises when it came to scanning time. I didn't have any surprises when it came to lamb marking.

" We knew we had fertile, productive animals and we knew that because we'd been measuring the whole way along. "

Course shaped by current research

The program's leaders want to make sure the course remains relevant at a time when farmers run a variety of wool and meat sheep breeds, especially to withstand the seasonal swings that come with climate change.

Emily King, who manages the course for AWI, says the latest sheep industry research data, collected over the past decade, is being analysed and will feed into the course from mid-year.

Emily King says the latest sheep data will feed into the course. (Supplied: Emily King)

"We really want to try and make sure we can optimise and target nutrition really specifically to different stages of the reproductive cycle," she says.

For Diana Tait, making good day-to-day decisions sets up her long-term goals that stretch well beyond her life on the farm.

"I've got two little young kids at home that are eight and five and it could potentially be a fifth-generation farm," she says.

" Whatever changes we can make now are only going to benefit them down the track. "

The course group learns how to condition score a mob of sheep at a property near Balmoral. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

World.title: Sabastian Sawe ran the marathon in an 'unbelievable time'. Here's why we can believe in it
World.content:
When Sabastian Sawe broke the tape on The Mall on Sunday, having run the London Marathon in a stunning 1 hour 59 minutes and 30 seconds, Steve Cram was speaking for so many gob-smacked running fans.

"That, you would say, is unbelievable, but we have just seen it," the former track world champion said on the BBC.

"Nobody has ever done this. They said it couldn't be done."

Any time the word "unbelievable" is used in a sporting context, an alarm bell normally starts ringing.

Even those who resolutely channel the X-Files' Agent Fox Mulder in their desperation to believe in the impossible sometimes need some level-headed Sherlock Holmesian pessimism as the only rational discourse — accepting the most likely explanation as the real truth.

Kenyan distance running has a new king in Sabastian Sawe. (Getty Images: Alex Davidson)

Athletics is not alone in being plagued by doping scandals, with performances being questioned time and time again in recent years across a multitude of sports, but it has had a particularly bad run of late.

Women's world record holder, Ruth Chepngetich, is serving a three-year ban for testing positive for the banned diuretic hydrochlorothiazide.

Chepngetich predictably denied any wrongdoing, somewhat inexplicably saying she had taken some of her housemaid's medication after feeling hot and having a rapid resting heartbeat.

Athletics Integrity Unit investigators, having studied her text messages and determined that the doping was likely intentional, found her baffling claims to be "hardly credible".

The Kenyan had stunned the world when she ran the Chicago Marathon in 2 hours, 9 minutes, and 56 seconds, almost 2 minutes faster than the previous world record, prompting many to call it "unbelievable".

Ruth Chepngetich has been disgraced after testing positive for a banned diuretic. (Getty Images: Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service/Tess Crowley)

That record still stands — albeit with a suitably-sized asterisk next to it — because the positive test came some time after the run.

In fact, it was days before she was due to run in the 2025 London Marathon that Chepngetich's cheating was exposed when she was a late withdrawal.

That's not the only bombshell cheating claim to come to light in recent months.

Paris Olympian Jackline Sakilu was banned for a massive 10 years after evidence the Tanzanian athlete had microdosed androsterone and etiocholanolone over long periods of time, including during the Paris Games.

So, when anyone describes a performance as "unbelievable", it's perhaps worth having a closer look.

Fortunately for those who hope to believe what they saw on the streets of London on Sunday, Sawe is one of those who has been asking for a closer look too.

Both Sabastian Sawe and Yomif Kejelcha beat the two-hour mark. (Getty Images: Warren Little)

Sawe has spoken out in the past about problems with doping in the sport of marathon running.

And, rather than just cast out phrases of disappointment, he has acted on it, too.

Given Kenya's woeful recent record on doping, the 30-year-old took the extraordinary step of calling for himself to be tested more regularly, inviting the Athletics Integrity Unit to test him as often as possible.

Last year, it did so, 25 times in fact, in the run-up to his attempt at the record in the 2025 Berlin Marathon — an attempt he was on track for before the hot conditions caused him to drop back in pace and settle for the win.

"The main reason was to show that I am clean, and I am doing it the right way," he said at the time.

The record will be subject to the usual ratification procedures before it is confirmed by World Athletics, and given the unpleasant track record of athletes, there's no telling if this astonishing run was completely legitimate.

But British Olympic champion Mo Farah seems convinced.

"We've waited long enough to see a human go sub-two," he said, perhaps alluding to the robot runners of China that recently broke the human half marathon world record.

"That's always been the question that we've asked. We've just witnessed something incredible."

How fast did Sawe run?

Sabastian Sawe with the now-traditional Monty Python-esque holding up of the shoe. (Getty Images: Karwai Tang)

A milestone-shattering record of this magnitude needs to be put into its appropriate context.

First up, some history.

The two-hour mark has been seen as the holy grail of marathon running, the limit of human capability in much the same way that the four-minute mile was in the immediate post-World War II era.

It was such a pivotal mark that INEOS was reported to have spent upwards of $20 million on its INEOS 1:59 Challenge in 2019.

There, double Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge did beat the two-hour mark in a run conducted under extreme time-trial conditions, with a laser-guided tracker and rotating pace makers, meaning World Athletics was never going to ratify the time.

But this was in a genuine race — arguably the biggest of them all — the London Marathon.

The time Sawe ran was more than a minute faster than the late Kelvin Kiptum's previous record of 2:00:35, set in 2023.

Incidentally, Kiptum also held the London Marathon course record of 2:01:25.

Sabastian Sawe declared himself sporting royalty on the streets of London. (Getty Images: Anadolu/Marcin Nowak)

Earlier in the week, Sawe had told the BBC he was keen to go fast and that it was "only a matter of time" before he broke Kiptum's world record.

He added, "I hope and wish one day [it will be me]" to be the one to break the two-hour barrier.

He wasn't the only person to do so on Sunday, but the man who finished behind him, marathon debutant Yomif Kejelcha, also broke the near-mythical record, finishing runner-up in 1:59:41, both men pushing each other to greater heights.

That says it all about how good the conditions were — light winds and temperatures in the mid-teens are ideal for marathon running.

Earlier in the day, Tigst Assefa of Ethiopia broke her own women's-only world record en route to victory, crossing the finish line in 2:15.41, beating the record of 2:15.50 she set last year in London.

This is slower than Chepngetich's all-time record because faster elite men can act as pacemakers for women when the races start at the same time.

Tigst Assefa celebrated her own world record with some shoe doodling too. (Getty Images: WireImage/Karwai Tang)

London's flat and fast course has just 75m of elevation gain over 42.2km, similar to Berlin (73m) and Chicago (74m), perennial record-chasing hot spots among marathon majors. Add a generational talent and the latest of adidas' super shoes, and you have a recipe for sub-two-hour success.

Adidas one-run-and-done shoe sets new mark in sport's arms race Adidas's new running shoe helped Ethiopia's Tigst Assefa take more than 2 minutes off the marathon world record in Berlin at the weekend — but if you want to get hold of the one-run-and-done shoe, you'd better start saving.

But even so, this was remarkable.

"There are things that happen in sport, and you want to be there to see history being made," Cram said.

"Roger Bannister [running] the first ever four-minute mile — those who were there on that day still tell that story today.

"We said it was a day for records, but I don't think in our wildest dreams we could have foreseen this."

What does that mean for your average punter?

Sabastian Sawe and Tigst Assefa broke the men's and women's world record. (Getty Images: Alex Davidson)

Watching a marathon on TV can be desperately misleading — men and women running alongside each other give barely any reference point to show how fast they are actually going.

Standing on course, catching a glimpse of these wisp-like runners blur through a gap between the crowds shows what TV cannot — an insane level of continuous speed that's hard to immediately fathom.

Imagine going down to your local parkrun — which is 5km — and reeling off a time of 14 minutes and 10 seconds. For the record, the average time for an Aussie to complete a parkrun is 33:31.

That's what time Sawe averaged for each 5km of his marathon. However, he did that pace for eight parkruns in a row without a break, then ran another half-distance parkrun for good measure.

Incredibly, he actually ran the second half of his run faster than his first, a phenomenon known as negative splitting.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

He went through the first 21 kilometres in 60:29 but put the hammer down for the second half marathon to record a time of just 59:01 — incidentally, only 63 men in history have run a half marathon on its own as quickly as that.

His last 5km block before the finale, from 35km to 40km, was run in 13:42.

Again, for comparison's sake, the fastest ever 5km parkrun stands at 13:44, set by Irish teenager Nick Griggs at the Belfast Victoria parkrun on November 9. The fastest in Australia is James Hansen's 13:53.

"This will reverberate around the world," Paula Radcliffe, a former record holder for the women's marathon, told BBC Sport.

"The goalposts have literally just moved for marathon running and where you benchmark yourself as being world class.

"It is a lesson to everybody out there. We say, 'Don't go out too fast' — they went out smartly and paced it really well."

World.title: King Charles heads to US for Trump state visit after shooting incident
World.content:
Reflecting about his first visit to the United States in 1970, King Charles III has previously said that "they were trying to marry me off to Tricia Nixon" — the then-president's eldest daughter.

Charles was 21 at the time. This week, the 77-year-old will return to the US for his first state visit as the British monarch, along with his wife, Queen Camilla.

Trump dinner shooting live updates: For the latest news on the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner shooting, read our blog.

These days, his focus is on trying to repair the so-called "special relationship" between the UK and the US, which is under significant strain, thanks to a growing spat between US President Donald Trump and British Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer over the war in the Middle East.

His Majesty's Government — which advised King Charles to accept Mr Trump's invitation to visit the US — is hoping soft power will help in these hard times, but the visit is proving controversial among British people.

"The optics of King Charles III travelling to the United States and shaking hands with Donald Trump whilst Donald Trump is waging a war against Iran is horrible at best," royal commentator Afua Hagan told the ABC.

"But conversely, we do need someone to smooth over the relationship between the United States and the United Kingdom, and King Charles III is our diplomat-in-chief. He's very good at, sort of, walking that tightrope."

Tricia Nixon chats with Charles, then the Prince of Wales, during the royal's 1970 visit to the US. (Getty Images: David Cairns/Daily Express/Hulton Archive)

It will also come in the wake of a shooting at a press gala in Washington, in which Mr Trump and other members of his US administration were the likely targets, according to acting US Attorney-General Todd Blanche.

"Following discussions on both sides of the Atlantic through the day, and acting on advice of Government, we can confirm the State Visit by Their Majesties will proceed as planned," a Palace spokesperson said after the incident.

"The King and Queen are most grateful to all those who have worked at pace to ensure this remains the case and are looking forward to the Visit getting underway."

The talks reportedly touched on security around the King and Queen's four-day visit, and to what degree the "events of Saturday evening may or may not impact on the operational planning for the visit".

Britons concerns about state visit

Since the US and Israel launched an attack on Iran in late February, Mr Trump has frequently singled out Britain and Sir Keir personally for failing to support the offensive.

He has described the PM as "not Winston Churchill" and Britain's aircraft carriers as "toys", while also threatening to unpick trade deals and pull out of the NATO defence alliance with European allies.

At the same time though, the president's gushing praise for King Charles has continued. Ahead of the visit he described the monarch as "a great gentleman", "a friend", and "a fantastic person".

Last week, Mr Trump told the BBC the royal visit could help repair US-UK relations.

"Absolutely. He's fantastic. He's a fantastic man," he said of the king. "Absolutely, the answer is yes [it could help relations].

"I know him well, I've known him for years. He's a brave man, and he's a great man. They would absolutely be a positive."

Nevertheless, some Britons are worried. Public opinion is divided about the visit. Opinion polls in the UK show Mr Trump is deeply unpopular, and some politicians have said it should be called off.

"[Trump] is a dangerous and corrupt gangster, and that is how we must treat him," Liberal Democrats party leader Sir Ed Davey told the parliament this month.

"I really fear for what Trump might say or do while our king is forced to stand by his side. We cannot put His Majesty in that position."

Donald Trump invited King Charles and Queen Camilla to the US. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

US-UK relationship 'still working' despite tensions

Outside Buckingham Palace in London, the ABC spoke to people who were both for and against the visit.

"It's really shocking for me that the King of Britain is visiting someone so extreme in his actions, in his views," Jamie from Gloucestershire said.

Abhinav, 32, from London, said the king should not take the trip.

"If the king goes to meet Donald Trump, it would pre-emptively be reinforcing Donald Trump's behaviour to keep bullying other countries and Donald Trump would inevitably feel that he can keep on doing what he's doing," he told the ABC.

Jacob, 20, said he could see the diplomatic value in the trip.

"I think the king's trying to keep the UK's relations with America in check, so I think it's good to go, but I wouldn't be surprised if there's a lot of backlash towards the trip," he said.

Peter, 28, from the Midlands, told the ABC he thought that "if there's anybody who can get through to Trump, I do think it would be the king".

"But if the US keeps doing what they're doing … we need to draw a line and focus on the Commonwealth, on Europe, and try and rebuild those bridges that we broke, with like Brexit," he added.

Trump's war has Starmer looking to Europe Keir Starmer was never a fan of Brexit. Now, under the cover of the war in Iran and a fractured US relationship, he's looking to Europe to return Britain to the fold.

Luke Coffey, senior fellow at the Hudson Institute foreign policy think tank in Washington DC, said he had confidence the US-UK relationship would endure despite Mr Trump's criticisms of Sir Keir.

"Right now, we're in one of these periods of time where we have a completely different worldview from the prime minister and the president, and we have a president who's very outspoken about such matters," Mr Coffey said.

"But this doesn't mean that below the surface that relationship still isn't working, and from what I can tell, speaking to officials, it's still very much working.

"The cooperation is still taking place. The dialogue is still happening. The intelligence is still being shared. And this is what matters at the end of the day."

Mr Coffey said he thought the king's visit would go some way to softening the president's rhetoric about Britain though.

"[Trump] probably sees His Majesty as someone far more influential and important on the British political system than he actually is in a constitutional monarchy," Mr Coffey said.

"But that doesn't matter because in President Trump's mind, the king matters, and if President Trump and the king get along, then it's very likely that problems with His Majesty's government will be sorted."

King Charles and Queen Camilla hosted Donald and Melania Trump during their state visit last year. (Pool: Doug Mills/The New York Times via Reuters)

King Charles and Queen Camilla will spend four days in the US. The trip has been timed to mark the 250th anniversary of US independence from Britain, but all eyes will be on whether Charles can reset relations at this point in time.

"The visit … recognises the challenges the United Kingdom, the United States, and our allies face across the world," a Buckingham Palace spokesperson said.

"This visit is a moment to reaffirm and renew our bilateral ties as we address those challenges together, in the UK's national interest."

The king and queen will arrive in the US on Monday, local time. The president and First Lady Melania Trump will host the royal couple for a private tea in Washington DC.

On Tuesday, the king will address a joint sitting of Congress, becoming just the second British monarch to do so following his mother Queen Elizabeth II in 1991. A state dinner will be held at the White House that evening.

During the visit, the king and president will hold a bilateral meeting, as will the queen and first lady.

The royal couple will also visit New York, Virginia, and Bermuda, a British overseas territory where he is the head of state.

Mr Trump and the first lady have twice embarked on state visits to the UK. Their most recent was in September last year, when they were hosted at Windsor Castle.

Queen Elizabeth II makes a point to the joint session of Congress in 1991. (Reuters: Rick Wilking)

Some American politicians and activists have said the king should meet with victims of the late convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein during the visit.

The king's brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, had a long-standing friendship with Epstein and is currently being investigated by British police for his links to the disgraced financier.

The family of Virginia Giuffre, one of the most prominent Epstein survivors said, "we strongly urge King Charles to meet with us and survivors and hear what we have to say".

Buckingham Palace has said this will not be possible because it might impact potential legal action.

"It would be so important for the king to sit down with the survivors and just acknowledge the pain they went through, especially given his brother was allegedly involved," Democratic Congressman Ro Khanna told the BBC.

"He doesn't have to discuss the specifics of his brother's case but he could show that the modern monarch actually listens."

Queen Camilla is expected to meet organisations advocating for survivors of domestic abuse during the trip, though the details of that meeting are not being released.

World.title: Magnitude-6.1 earthquake and raging wildfires strike Japan's north
World.content:
A preliminary magnitude-6.1 earthquake struck northern Japan early on Monday, local time, the US Geological Survey has reported, but there are no immediate reports of fatalities or damage.

The earthquake struck at 5:24am, 18 kilometres west of the small town of Sarabetsu in Hokkaido at a depth of 81km.

Last Monday, a magnitude-7.7 earthquake off northern Japan sparked a short-lived tsunami alert and an advisory of a slightly higher risk of a possible mega-quake for its coastal areas.

The warning triggered widespread evacuation orders, affecting about 170,000 people.

Fires in north continue to rage

The recent quake came after Japan deployed 1,400 firefighters ‌and dozens of Self-Defense Force personnel to battle mountain blazes that have been raging in the north for five days, threatening to reach homes in the coastal town of Otsuchi.

Fanned by dry, windy weather, two ​more wildfires broke out elsewhere in the north on Sunday.

A helicopter conducts firefighting operations in Otsuchi. (Reuters: Kim Kyung-Hoon)

One in Kitakata city and ​the other in Nagaoka, potentially stretching firefighting resources thin as local authorities send personnel ⁠to neighbouring areas.

The area burned by the Otsuchi fires reached 1,373 hectares as of Sunday morning, ​up 7 per cent from a day earlier.

Residents forced to evacuate

The fires threaten residential districts of Otsuchi on the Pacific Coast — a town that lost nearly a 10th of its population in one of Japan's worst disasters, the March 2011 earthquake and tsunami.

Authorities expanded the scope of evacuation orders to 1,558 households or 3,257 residents by Sunday evening, roughly a third ​of Otsuchi's population.

"Although the Self-Defense Forces are fighting the fires from the sky [with helicopters], the dry weather and ​winds are helping the fires expand," Otsuchi Mayor Kozo Hirano told a press conference.

The area burned by the Otsuchi fires reached 1,373 hectares as of Sunday morning. (Reuters: Kim Kyung-Hoon)

Some residents used hoses to spray water ‌onto ⁠their houses and surrounding foliage, hoping to keep the flames at bay.

"I am prepared to evacuate by my car at any time. Fire won't be able to catch up to us since it does not move as fast as a tsunami," said 67-year-old resident Shigeki Fujiwara.

Flames up in the mountain were visible from his ​home, and while his family ​had already been evacuated, ⁠he said he had chosen to stay behind because he was worried about the house.

Cause of fire under investigation

The only casualty to date has been one minor injury ​suffered when a person fell at an evacuation centre, Japan's Fire and Disaster ​Management Agency said ⁠on its website.

Climate ​change has increased the frequency Japan's wildfires. (Reuters: Kim Kyung-Hoon)

Rain is expected in some parts of Iwate prefecture's southern coastal region, where Otsuchi is located, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.

The cause of the Otsuchi fires is not clear and is under investigation.

While Japan ⁠has experienced ​relatively few wildfires compared with other parts of the world, climate ​change has increased their frequency, especially as the early spring months before the humid rainy season have been hot, dry and with winds ​that can whip up flames.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Mental impairment law falling short for man found not guilty but imprisoned
World.content:
West Australian legal experts say the Criminal Law Mental Impairment (CLMI) Act is not working as intended, citing a case in Broome where a man was found not criminally responsible for murder but was still jailed.

The first Supreme Court case to be tried under the new act, held more than 2,000 kilometres from Perth, has raised concerns about the state's ability to implement its principles.

A Kimberley man, who killed his foster brother in 2023 in front of family members, was found not guilty by way of mental impairment.

Despite the fact Ian Ralph Brooke was not criminally responsible, a court heard earlier this month that he will spend an indefinite amount of time in prison.

Justice Peter Quinlan concluded it was "impossible" to fully apply the act's principles in sentencing, as required by law.

Peter Quinlan says it is impossible for him to give effect to a number of principles under the act. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

Not guilty but imprisoned

The CLMI Act took effect in late 2024 and replaced controversial laws governing the management of people, with significant mental impairments, who are accused of crimes.

Mr Brooke's case was eligible to be considered under the new act, making it the first Supreme Court special hearing of its kind in WA.

Much of the sentencing centred on what Justice Quinlan and counsel described as a "catch-22" where a custody order was the only option due to the lack of secure hospitals.

Mr Brooke was given a custody order for the duration of his life and the Mental Impairment Review Tribunal will decide where he serves it, subject to periodic review.

"Unless … there is some transformative change to the number and nature of declared places in this state, I recognise Mr Brooke will remain in a prison," Justice Quinlan said.

"Subject to an identical regime of management, control and discipline as prisoners who have been convicted and sentenced for criminal offences.

"This conclusion means it is impossible for me to give effect to the number of principles that I am required to by law."

These principles include imposing the least restrictive option available and ensuring the "best possible treatment, care and support".

The court heard this would have been a secure hospital, followed by a gradual transition into community.

The reformed CLMI Act took effect in late 2024. (ABC Perth: Alicia Bridges)

Lack of facilities

The only forensic hospital in the state is the 30-bed Frankland Centre, which opened in 1993.

A forensic hospital is for prisoners who need mental health rehabilitation and clinical care.

Despite WA's prison population more than quadrupling since the opening of the centre, there are still only 30 beds and a 20-person waitlist.

Luke Cassidy provides free legal advice to people with mental illnesses. (Supplied)

Ruah Legal Services principal lawyer Luke Cassidy said this was a "human rights crisis happening right now".

"Those objects, principles and intentions are undermined by the chronic under-resourcing of many of the agencies involved with implementing the legislation," he said.

"We need action if we want to get our waitlist down and treat these people with dignity and respect."

Forensic psychiatrist Rajan Darjee testified in Mr Brooke's case, saying prisons were places for "punishment and containment" of criminals and not for treating and rehabilitating the mentally unwell.

"Every civilised jurisdiction I know of in the world has secure hospitals, and they send people in his position to hospital because that is right from a clinical perspective, a human rights perspective, and also from a legal perspective," Dr Darjee said.

"I've not come across a jurisdiction, or rarely [have] … where secure hospital treatment is not what happens for someone charged with murder who has a severe mental illness."

WA's prison population has quadrupled since the Frankland Centre opened. (ABC Perth: Alicia Bridges)

Competing interests

Acting Attorney-General Paul Papalia dismissed the notion the law had not been fully followed.

"Whether they're released into the community has to be dictated by whether it's safe, so there's two competing interests," he said.

He acknowledged there were no available beds in the Frankland Centre and demand was greater than capacity.

"In our prison system we have people who are mentally unwell who might be suitable to be housed in the Frankland Centre," Mr Papalia said.

"If there's no capacity we have to look after them in the prison system and we do care for people who are mentally unwell in the prison."

Paul Papalia says if there is no capacity in the Frankland Centre then people need to be cared for in prison. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

During Mr Brooke's sentencing the court heard he was in custody for 10 months before he was seen by a psychiatrist and prescribed antipsychotic medication.

The lawyers and judge in this case all agreed WA's prison system significantly lacked the capability to provide mental health care, citing overstretched and overworked staff.

In a statement, Health Infrastructure Minister John Carey said 32 new sub-acute male forensic mental health beds were in the process of being established.

Until the beds become available, people like Mr Brooke, with serious mental illness, may continue to be held in prison with the forensic hospital's capacity exhausted.

World.title: Missing 5yo Alice Springs girl believed to be abducted, police say
World.content:
Northern Territory Police say they are now treating the disappearance of a five-year-old girl in Alice Springs as an abduction, while searching for a 47-year-old man who they believe can assist with their inquiries.

Police say the girl — referred to as Sharon — was reported missing by her family at about 1:30am on Sunday, after she could not be found at her home on Marshall Court in the Old Timers Aboriginal town camp.

They say she was last seen by family when she was put to bed just before 11:30pm on Saturday.

Five-year-old Sharon was reported missing from the Old Timers town camp in Alice Springs on Sunday morning. (Supplied: NT Police Force)

In an update to the media on Monday, Acting Commander Mark Grieve said police believed the five-year-old had been abducted from her home.

Acting Commander Grieve said the man they were looking for Jefferson Lewis had recently been released from prison and was believed to have been staying at the house the girl went missing from early on Sunday morning.

Police say they are looking for Jefferson Lewis in relation to Sharon's disappearance. (Supplied: NT Police Force)

"He currently remains one of the few people who were in Old Timers Camp at the time and who has not made themselves known to police, nor have police been able to locate him," he said.

" We do believe Sharon has been abducted." "

Acting Commander Grieve said Mr Lewis had not been in prison for child-related offending and was not believed to be closely related to Sharon or her family.

"He's the only person that we haven't been able to locate and speak to who was in and around that area at the time," he said.

"Considering himself and Sharon went missing at around about the same time, it certainly brings about those suspicious circumstances and we'd like to speak to him about that."

Mark Grieve says police believe Sharon has been abducted. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

Acting Commander Grieve said police were "wrapping around" Sharon's mother and providing her with support.

"Obviously it's a terrible situation to have such a young child go missing," he said.

"We're over 24 hours now so it'd certainly be my worst nightmare as a parent."

Acting Commander Grieve repeated calls for public assistance to find the five-year-old.

Officers from NT Police and the NT Emergency Service are searching for Sharon. (ABC News: Will Green )

"Please, if you've got any information, regardless of how small in detail you think it may be, please let us know," he said.

"You just don't know what piece of information might complete the jigsaw puzzle.

"We want to find Sharon healthy and we want to get her back to her family."

Earlier this morning, police said officers had resumed foot searches after they were unable to locate the five-year-old overnight.

Live Moment NT Police provided an update on their investigation into Sharon's disappearance. Press conference ends That's all for the relatively short press conference. But the ABC will continue to bring you updates on this developing story as they come to hand. A 'worst nightmare' scenario Acting Commander Grieve has reiterated calls for assistance from the public to help find Sharon. "Obviously it's a terrible situation to have such a young child go missing," he said. "We're over 24 hours now so it'd certainly be my worst nightmare as a parent." Mr Grieve says police are "wrapping around" the five-year-old's mother to provide support. "We've actually facilitated some other accommodation just to provide her with some extra support," he said. "Please, if you've got any information, regardless of how small in detail you think it may be, please let us know. "You just don't know what piece of information might complete the jigsaw puzzle. "We want to find Sharon healthy and we want to get her back to her family." Man 'went missing' at around the same time Acting Commander Grieve says the man police are searching for in relation to Sharon's disappearance was not in prison for child-related offending before his recent release. Acting Commander Grieve says police don't believe the 47-year-old was "directly related" to the five-year-old, but may have "a very peripheral link" to her family. "He was in and around the house at that point in time so I'm assuming there was some sort of recognition of who he may be," he said. "He's the only person that we haven't been able to locate and speak to who was in and around that area at the time. "Considering himself and Sharon went missing at around about the same time, it certainly brings about those suspicious circumstances and we'd like to speak to him about that. "If he is involved, we certainly hope that no harm has come to Sharon." Show more

What we know

Police say they believe Sharon likely wandered off through an unlocked door after being put to bed, with her mother raising the alarm after checking her room and finding her missing.

"Her mother went back to check on her and her mother was the one that telephoned police," Acting Superintendent Michael Ordelman said yesterday.

" But what concerned initial reporting members is that the [Old Timers Camp] is adjacent to the Todd River … where it's quite easy for a child to wander away and not be easily locatable. "

Emergency Service members have been searching the Todd River. (ABC News: Will Green )

At the time, she was wearing a dark blue, short-sleeved T-shirt with a white ring stripe around the neck and cuffs and a pair of black boxer-style underwear.

Acting Superintendent Ordelman also said police had not been able to find some other members of the Old Timers Camp.

"We're not saying that's nefarious, but as I said, we're not ruling out anything," he said.

But due to the prolonged length of time Sharon had been missing, Acting Superintendent Ordelman said police had "mounting concerns" and pleaded for help from the public.

More than 50 police officers are searching for Sharon. (ABC News: Will Green)

"It's a very broad investigation at this stage where we're not ruling out anything, but police obviously have concerns because of the time it's taking [and] the age of young Sharon," he said.

"We don't know if she has access to water. There's some areas she may have gone to find water, but the increasing passage of time is concerning.

"We'd like anyone in the community that knows anything, however insignificant they think it is, to contact police so we can find her, locate her, return her to her family."

Police say they are "not ruling out anything" after they were unable to find some residents of the Old Timers Camp. (ABC News: Will Green )

As of yesterday afternoon, Acting Superintendent Ordelman said there were more than 50 police officers searching for Sharon, along with members of the NT Emergency Service.

"A police helicopter has been [deployed] and has got a police spotter on it," he said.

"Search and Rescue from Darwin has provided resources and there's a search master currently assisting with the investigation.

" Emergency services have come in to assist. A police dog has tried to locate a track to locate young Sharon. That's been unsuccessful at this stage. "

Members of NT Police's elite Territory Response Group are expected to travel from Darwin to join the search this morning, with investigators urging anyone with information to call 131 444 and quote reference number P26120934.

World.title: Maccas wins battle to set up in 'world's coolest street'
World.content:
McDonald's has won a court battle to build a 24/7 fast-food restaurant in a Melbourne shopping strip named the world's coolest street in 2024.

Darebin Council last year rejected a planning application for the restaurant in High Street in Northcote, arguing it did not fit with the character of the area.

The council's decision to reject the application at a meeting in November was applauded by residents who had gathered in the chamber for the vote.

That decision has now been overturned by the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) after McDonald's appealed against the Darebin Council ruling.

Opponents to the McDonald's restaurant argue the proposal would not fit the "cool vibe" of the area. (ABC News: Stephanie Anderson)

High Street, Northcote was named the "world's coolest street" by Time Out magazine in 2024, with the magazine praising its "unique" local businesses.

The site of the proposed restaurant, at 323 High Street, has been empty for more than a year, after a fire.

More than 11,000 people had signed an online petition against the McDonald's restaurant, which argued the restaurant would "compromise Northcote's unique character".

"Continuing, fast-food establishments like McDonald's typically lead to an increase in litter, undesirable traffic congestion, and environmental concerns tied to such a high-volume business model," the petition said.

However, VCAT member Michael Deidun said the tribunal could not reject the application purely because it was being made by a fast-food giant.

"This Tribunal does not have the power to review the corporate approach of McDonalds, its work practices and ethics, the type of food it produces, its impact on human health, or whether it fits the 'cool' vibes of its context," he said.

Several communities have fought plans by McDonald's to set up restaurants in their area. (ABC Radio Brisbane: Anna Levy)

McDonald's Australia said it welcomed the decision by VCAT, arguing the site was already zoned for commercial use.

"The restaurant represents an investment of more than $2 million and reflects McDonald's ongoing commitment to employment-generating development across Victoria," the fast-food operator said.

"The restaurant will be owned and operated by a local franchisee, who will contribute to the local area through employment, access to training and development opportunities, and supporting local community organisations."

'It'll change the vibe of High Street'

McDonald's Australia said the development would generate 100 jobs during construction and a further 100 full-time, part-time and casual jobs once operational.

"We look forward to joining Northcote and playing an active role in the local community when the restaurant opens later this year," it said.

Northcote resident Matt Atanasovski hopes the McDonald's restaurant does not hurt local businesses. (ABC News)

Northcote resident Jo Pugh said she was disappointed that the council's decision to reject the application was overturned.

Phillip Island McDonald's backlash The fast food giant is facing backlash after lodging a planning permit application to build a new restaurant in tourist hotspot Cowes.

"I think it's a poor decision. There are plenty of McDonald's around this area generally in the surrounding suburbs and I don't think we need a McDonald's in High Street," she said.

"It'll change the vibe of High Street, bring a different demographic in."

Another Northcote local, Matt Atanasovski, said he had mixed feelings as he thought the restaurant might bring people to the area.

"I guess Maccas isn't necessarily cool so it will be a bit of an eyesore for the street," he said.

"My hope is that it doesn't take away from the local businesses who are very much struggling here on High Street because of our economy."

World.title: 'She's like Will Ferrell': Why Kitty Flanagan said yes to Anne Edmonds
World.content:
Anne Edmonds was performing a show with the Melbourne Theatre Company when she was struck with the idea for her latest comedy series Bad Company — an unfettered satire of the arts world.

Fast Facts about Bad Company What: A sharp comedy with heart featuring two of Australia's comedy greats going head-to-head. Starring: Anne Edmonds, Kitty Flanagan, Angella Dravid, Cameron James, Will Gibb, Kira Puru and Ben Pfeiffer. Where: On ABC iview. Most likely to make you feel: That no-one could satirise the arts world quite like Eddo.

Edmonds says her musical debut as a wily aged care manager in Tom Gleisner's 2023 production of Bloom was an "amazing experience".

"But, after spending a lot of time in that building, I was like, '[The theatre] feels like the perfect place to set a sit-com," she laughs.

The AACTA-winning comedian didn't just create and write Bad Company. She also stars in the six-part series as artistic director Margie Argyle, who's run her beloved "Papa's" avant-garde theatre into the ground in her six short years at the helm.

This is unsurprising, given Margie Argie is more interested in gyrating across the floor and putting on insufferable one-woman shows starring herself than anything real audiences would pay to see.

With the future of The Argyle Theatre in peril, the board installs restrained chief executive Julia McNamara (Kitty Flanagan) to turn things around. Of course, J Mac is a "neoliberal wet dream" of a corporate robot who's never even heard of Henrik Ibsen (ahem, the father of modern drama).

Adding insult to Margie's injury, one of Julia's cost-cutting ideas involves axing the costume department and buying ready-made get-ups from Spotlight. (ABC/Guesswork Television: Sarah Enticknap)

Cue clashes over everything from the merits of having a dedicated perruquier (AKA wig-maker) on staff, to whether or not they should stage a production of Grease to keep the lights on.

At the mercy of each of their whims is a supporting cast including comedians Angella Dravid, Cameron James and Will Gibb, musician Kira Puru and actor Ben Pfeiffer (as the aforementioned perruquier).

Loading...

Facing The Argyle's closure, will the ensemble find a way to work together despite backstage chaos and their differences? Will Margie learn to listen to other people, and Julia to express herself freely?

You can probably guess where the story's going already.

Edmonds and Flanagan had good company on set, supported by comics Angella Dravid and Cameron James, along with quietly hilarious actor Ben Pfeiffer. (ABC/Guesswork Television: Sarah Enticknap)

But Bad Company was never about reinventing the sit-com.

" Characters are what I'm interested in most of all," Edmonds says. "My vision was: 'How do I make these characters as strong as they can be?' "

In many ways, the series feels like the culmination of all the painstaking persona work she's done her entire career.

Rounding out the comedian-heavy cast is Will Gibb, who brings to life Julia's lost, naive son Ryan. (ABC/Guesswork Television: Sarah Enticknap)

It all started with the Melbourne comedy circuit

Bursting onto the stand-up scene during the 2010 iteration of the Melbourne Comedy Festival's RAW open mic competition, it didn't take long for Edmonds to gain notoriety for her cutting observations of the inner-city suburban Australian psyche.

Stream Bad Company now on ABC iview Margie, the unstable artistic director of the iconic theatre company, The Argyle, is up for the fight of her life, when Julia is hi-jacked from her corporate career to save the place from financial ruin.

By 2017, she was winning awards for her portrayal of unhinged fashion and beauty expert Helen Bidou, who featured on breakfast TV satire Get Krack!n. The comic returned to our screens that same year with The Edge of the Bush, an original miniseries Edmonds created, wrote — and played a casual four characters in.

But the critically acclaimed absurd tale of a calisthenics dynasty rocked by an incest scandal was constrained by five episodes that were 10 minutes long, and saw just one season.

Margie and her colleagues are given significantly more time to develop in Bad Company.

Edmonds based Margie on a mix of people she's met in the arts, with a bit of herself thrown in: "My partner would probably say going from 'fine' to 'not fine' very quick." (ABC/Guesswork Television: Sarah Enticknap)

And in dedicating herself to the complex artistic director — who is simultaneously the embodiment of cringe, deeply irresponsible, deceptively manipulative, and a good person who is struggling — Edmonds was able to extend herself in new ways.

"Margie is deluded, [it] is her main feature. [But] to give a character depth, you can't be silly the whole time. The hardest thing for me was to try and be earnest," she explains.

" My instinct as a comedian is to go for laughs always — trying to go for pathos makes me uncomfortable, but I'm glad I did it. "

That pathos — combined with a measured, confident supporting cast of familiar characters like Julia — is what elevates this show from a slapstick-lite series to a sharp comedy that centres human, complicated characters.

"Even though [Margie is] loose as a person, I worked really hard on keeping her in the real world as much as I could," Edmonds says. (ABC/Guesswork Television: Sarah Enticknap)

The Flanagan factor

Edmonds says she asked Fisk and Utopia star Kitty Flanagan to act alongside her in Bad Company before she started writing back in 2024.

Flanagan didn't even question what it was about before agreeing.

Julia was familiar territory for Flanagan, who quips the hardest thing about playing her was pretending to be good at finances: "That was some excellent acting from me." (ABC/Guesswork Television: Sarah Enticknap)

"I'm happy to work with Eddo on anything. She's one of the funniest people I know," explains the comedian, whose 2026 Melbourne Comedy Festival hour was nominated for the Most Outstanding Show award.

" I love her style of comedy. Unpredictable, slightly unhinged and with occasional bouts of random shouting … She's like Will Ferrell. "

Kitty Flanagan was initially told Fisk was too unlikeable. Now, her sitcom is an international fave The much-loved Australian comedian speaks about the hard road to getting her ABC TV sitcom Fisk made, and its international success.

And yet, Edmonds still thinks herself "extremely lucky" Flanagan said yes.

"It's obviously a real thrill for me, because she's one of my heroes," she continues.

"She and I have a similar background in wanting to make people laugh, and I've loved working with her [in the past]."

The success of Fisk, and all of Flanagan's experience making TV herself, also helped.

"She was very understanding of what I was trying to do, and going through."

'You'd think I'd have learned'

Producing a TV show you've created, written and starred in couldn't be more different to the comedy world Edmonds started in.

"The incredible thing about standup is you have an idea in your head and then you just say it into a microphone without a million processes in between," she laughs.

"There's a lot of people in the mix when you're making a TV show, and especially when you're making the first season of a TV show; everyone's got their own anxieties about it [and] wants it to be a certain way."

Loading Instagram content

Edmonds says she was in a "bit of shell shock" after making The Edge of the Bush, struggling to come to terms with the differences in the final version of the show.

She was more open-minded with Bad Company, but it was still quite an experience.

"You'd think I would have learned. Writing something on your own is hard. I seem to have done it again, and on a bigger scale."

Flanagan echoes this.

"One of the things I've learned is that it's a miracle any TV show ever gets made," she says.

"You need to really believe in your idea and trust you know what's funny. That's why Eddo is so good; she knows what's funny, you can trust her."

The comedian's faith in Edmonds was so unwavering that she made a point of asking her to show her exactly what she wanted from Julia.

"If I wasn't getting it right, I'd ask Eddo to say it for me," Flanagan says. "Some actors don't like a 'line read', but I love it."

A delicate balance

There's little about the performing arts world that goes unskewered in Bad Company — from the stereotypically delicate constitution of an actor to the concept of putting on a ridiculously long, foreign play without an intermission.

The line between poking fun at the arts world and outright mocking it, à la Timothée Chalamet and his viral comments about the opera and ballet, is a thin one.

But the gags all land, whether about marketing strategies that boil down to disseminating "copious totes", or Margie's repeated declarations of herself as a "storyteller, a truth custodian, a disruptor, a witch, a feminist, a mother" — in Helen-Bidou-coded fashion.

The "copious totes" in question. (ABC/Guesswork Television: Sarah Enticknap)

Only someone who deeply loves the arts, but has also spent a significant amount of time looking in on it, could satirise it so perfectly.

"I'm not someone who really grew up in the arts. I didn't do youth theatre or anything like that. I wish I had, but I didn't. I got into comedy when I was 28," Edmonds says.

After almost 20 years in the entertainment industry, she still thinks of herself as having "one foot in the arts and one foot in the real world".

"Sometimes in the artsy kind of left world, it's easy to go, 'Oh, everyone who works in banks is stupid and conservative, but I think that's too easy … So I tried to show that side of things.

"Theatres grapple with the line between making art and putting the lights on, and you have to talk about money, unfortunately. Julia's point of view is relevant, too."

By the end of the series, Edmonds hopes viewers love The Argyle Theatre and the people behind it as much as she loves the arts.

"Hopefully I haven't offended my theatre colleagues too much," she says.

"But the great thing about being in the arts is we have the capacity to reflect on ourselves."

World.title: ‘They may have lost money’: Melbourne house sells for just $500 above reserve
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘They may have lost money’: Melbourne house sells for just $500 above reserve Shona Hendley April 27, 2026 — 11:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

A family home in Reservoir in original condition on “a massive block” sold to a first home buyer for $900,500 at auction on Saturday, just $500 above its reserve. The three-bedroom, south-facing brick house at 22 Merrilands Road was on a 888-square-metre block, a short walk from Keon Park train station. It had a price guide of $850,000 to $915,000. Selling agent Keb Nguyen from Ray White Reservoir said the home sold for less than he expected. “The reserve was $900,000,” he said. “We’d thought we’d get a bit more.”



The auction opened at $800,000, with four active bidders up to the $830,0000-mark, when two dropped out. “The property was declared on the market at $900,000, and then there was one more bid of $500, and that was it,” Nguyen said. The 888-square-metre land was a drawcard for buyers. Ray White Reservoir He said while the property was dated, its large land size caught the eye of investors. “Many people saw the potential of the massive block and the home that could be renovated or expanded,” Nguyen said.



Related Article Auctions West Footscray house sells post-auction for $1,175,000 after passing in Ultimately, a first home buyer with plans to use the property as an investment was successful. “He is looking at what he needs to do to secure the grant and the deposit scheme, so he might have to move in for a bit before it can be used as an investment,” Nguyen said. The sellers, also investors, previously bought the property from Nguyen in 2022. “I think they may have lost money,” he said. “I sold it to them … for $860,000 plus tax.”



Stamp duty payable on the purchase would likely have been just under $47,000. The property was one of 246 scheduled auctions in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 56 per cent from 151 reported results, while 22 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. In Wollert, a two-bedroom house near powerlines sold at auction for $518,500, nearly $80,000 over its reserve, in a runaway auction. 1 Frisby Street was listed with a price guide of $400,000 to $440,000 and had a reserve of $440,000.



Related Article Property downsizing Holiday of a lifetime: Maria is going on a ‘golden gap year’ Selling agent Hayden Assaad from Ray White Wollert said he was “extremely surprised” by the result. “To be honest, we were not expecting to get that price whatsoever,” he said. “Being so close to the power lines, and with an electrical box behind it, I didn’t expect this result, but the person who wanted it was out for it the whole way.” Four bidders took part in the auction, among them a first home buyer and an investor.



“The investor ultimately purchased the home with a final bid of $500, after the first home buyer dropped out at $518,000,” Assaad said. The property was a “relatively new” two-storey home purchased by the vendor as a first home, he said. Records show it last sold in 2016 for $160,000. “[The vendor] looked after it really well, and I think that was one of the biggest draw cards: it was well presented and cared for,” he said. In Glen Waverley, a “unit the size of a house” sold at auction for $1.365 million.



1/18 Harvie Street had a price guide of $1.2 million to $1.3 million, with a reserve of $1.3 million. Grace Rodrigues from BigginScott Glen Waverley said there were four registered bidders but “only two really got into it”. “It opened with a bid of $1.2 million,” she said. “But the second bid of $1.3 million meant that the other two were priced out.” The following 10 minutes came down to a fight between a family aiming to secure a home in the Glen Waverley school zone and a downsizer, who was ultimately successful. “The dad really wanted it. He had tears in his eyes when he didn’t get it,” Rodrigues said.



Related Article Property market The type of home where prices are falling most right now As well as the location, Rodrigues said the 20-year-old property was “unique” because it was one of the last house-sized brick units built on larger blocks before townhouses really “took off”. “It has three-metre-high ceilings, a huge living area and big bedrooms. The land size is also really good,” she said. The lack of steps was also attractive to the downsizer. “As people get older, they don’t want stairs,” Rodrigues said. “So the fact that the garage’s interior access to the home was pretty flat was appealing.”



PRD chief economist Diaswati Mardiasmo said April was always a “weird time” for the auction market. “It’s after Easter, there’s an upcoming federal budget and Anzac Day is thrown in there too, it’s like an auction clearance rate soup,” she said. The economic climate, with recent rate rises, the war in the Middle East and rising living costs also had an impact. “There are already those seasonal things, and then this is thrown on top,” Mardiasmo said.

World.title: Unliveable house sells a second time after reno abandoned
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Unliveable house sells a second time after reno abandoned Sarah Webb April 27, 2026 — 11:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

A fire-ravaged home south of Brisbane that last sold a year ago for $400,000 has changed hands again, this time fetching $600,000 despite being unliveable. Partially rebuilt after its interstate owners abandoned their renovation plans, three bidders battled for the Kingston house on Sunday, with each banking on the land value in what’s become one of the city’s fastest-growing pockets. Marketed as a half-finished three-bedroom opportunity with all the kitchen materials included and ready for installation, the home, at 22 Ashvale Street, sits on a 600-square-metre corner block in a postcode where undeveloped blocks have become increasingly rare. Bidding opened at $400,000 with the three out of the five registered bidders trading steady $50,000 and $25,000 rises until $570,000. The auction then paused, with the property selling shortly after in negotiations.



Selling agent Ramin Bay, of Ray White Logan City, said the three bidders planned to finish the build and use the home as an investment. “They could see the capital growth potential – especially considering how rare blocks are there,” he said. The house at 22 Ashvale Street, Kingston, was marketed as a half-finished three-bedroom opportunity with all the kitchen materials included and ready for installation. Ray White Logan City “Kingston sits in the 4144 postcode which includes Woodridge and most of this area is now subdivided.” Domain’s latest house price data captured the eye-watering growth of the pocket, particularly in neighbouring Woodridge, where median house prices climbed 203.8 per cent in five years to $607,500. Kingston values also shot up, with medians rising 14.9 per cent in the past 12 months to $750,000.



Despite the uplift, Bay said the owners had made the tough choice to offload the home after finding the renovations too hard to manage from afar. “Even though they live in Sydney, they always believed in that area and while it wasn’t the first home they had renovated and sold, this one involved a lot more structural work,” he said. The bidders planned to finish the home and use it as an investment. Ray White Logan City “The bedrooms had a lot of fire damage and they took that away and demolished half of the house … but the house still needs a new bathroom and kitchen and basically everything.” But Bay said they had turned a profit.



The Kingston house was one of 64 scheduled auctions across South East Queensland. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary clearance rate of 37 per cent from 46 reported results, with seven homes withdrawn. In Kuraby, a 20-year-old estate in one of the suburb’s most tightly held blue-chip pockets smashed its reserve, selling for $2.381 million under the hammer on Sunday. The five-bedroom, three-bathroom house – at 32 Beris Crescent – attracted 10 registered bidders, with three upsizers competing. Set on a 748-square-metre block with a pool, shed and quality fittings, bidding opened at $1.8 million before quickly climbing past $2.38 million.



A family from a neighbouring suburb nabbed the keys. Selling agent Jacky Chu, of Place Sunnybank, said the vendors snapped up the home 10 years ago for $1.095 million, only making minor updates during that time. “The other auctions we had this weekend were a bit tougher, so this result tells us good and rare homes – even with market certainty – are still getting good interest,” he said. “The buyers live close by and have mum and dad with them, so they’re a multi-generational family, and they loved the upstairs and downstairs living options.” In Windsor, a first-home buyer snapped up a one-bedroom unit prior to auction for $703,000 amid soaring demand for the entry-level apartments.



The unit at 16/26 Le Geyt Street last sold for $523,000 two years ago, and for $312,000 in 2021. Selling agent Andy Flanagan, of Ray White Ascot, said that transaction timeline perfectly illustrated a major attitude shift towards the once-polarising one-bedder. “Ten years ago, first-home buyers used to steer clear of them,” he said. “But as two-bedroom units became more expensive, it really pushed people to them and created an opportunity.



“We ended up selling this one prior just because of how competitive it was. “The vendors had bought it as their first home and the buyer was a single bloke.” Flanagan said the home’s study space – which he described as one of the most sought-after features among one-bedroom unit buyers – fuelled demand. LJ Hooker chief of research Matthew Tiller said while the Easter and Anzac Day period had softened activity, listing volumes were beginning to recover. “We are seeing a slow uptick in the number of listings overall coming online after Easter and we will see that continue to grow over the coming months,” he said.



“But numbers still remain below average.” Tiller added that sentiment remained positive across South East Queensland, with a lack of new homes being built amid tight supply underpinning buyer confidence. World.title: Ticket to ride: Australian IS brides secure flights home
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWIslamic State Ticket to ride: Australian IS brides secure flights home Mostafa Rachwani and Paul Sakkal Updated April 27, 2026 — 11:00am ,first published April 27, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

A group of women and children linked to the Islamic State who have been attempting to return to Australia have plane tickets to Australia and hope to depart Damascus within the next few days. The group, which includes four women and nine children, are all Australian citizens. They left al-Roj camp in north-eastern Syria on Saturday. They had been detained there for seven years following the fall of the Islamic State caliphate. Members of Australian families at al-Roj Camp in eastern Syria prepare to leave for Damascus as part of a second repatriation effort. Baderkhan Ahmad (AP) A source close to the return process, which is not being facilitated by the government, confirmed to this masthead that the women and children had plane tickets to Australia and would be flying out of Damascus in coming days. The source asked to remain anonymous due to the sensitive nature of the situation.



The group intends to get on a plane in coming days but their path home remains uncertain. Authorities in Syria or stopover countries may attempt to block their journey. The group has been held in the camps since the fall of the so-called caliphate and the death or capture of their husbands and fathers, who allegedly fought for Islamic State. The al-Roj Camp in eastern Syria. AP It comes after Lana Hussein, an official with the women’s protection unit of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which manages the camp’s security, on Saturday said the four families were expected to be “deported under security procedures”. This is the second attempt by the group to return to Australia since February.





Advocates for the families say many were either children or young women pressured by their husbands at the time they left Australia. But the government has previously said security agencies believed the current cohort contained some particularly radical individuals, making it more risky than groups that had returned in previous years. A soldier stands guard as vehicles arrive at al-Roj Camp in eastern Syria to transport Australian families to Damascus as part of a second repatriation effort. AP In 2022, the Albanese government said it was incumbent on Australia to bring the group home to give them a chance at rehabilitation. Yet this year, at a moment when community attitudes towards migration are hardening and after the Bondi massacre sparked anxiety about extremism, Albanese has taken a more uncompromising approach, declaring the group had “made their bed” and that he would not actively help them to return. Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said on Monday he could not provide specific details about the group. “The Australian government is not repatriating these people. That’s where the matter stands and we’ve made this really clear. We’re not providing any support at all,” Marles said.



Earlier on Monday, deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume said the cohort’s return to Australia felt like a “foregone conclusion”. She accused the government of abdicating responsibility. “These are people that we know have actively left Australia and gone to join ISIS-linked terrorists overseas to fight against everything that Australians believe in: equality, the rule of law, democracy. Everything that we believe in, they are against. And yet, somehow this government has said it’s not our problem, it’s not our fault,” Hume told Sky News. “It’s up to [the government] now to explain what happens to these people when they come back, where they’re going to be settled, which suburbs are they going to be living in, and are there going to be any legal ramifications for their return?” Labor frontbencher Mark Butler said on Sky News’ Sunday Agenda: “If they manage to get to Australian borders and they have committed any crimes, they will be met by the full force of law at those borders.” Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, who has spoken regularly about the need to “shut the door” to extremists, on Sunday said Labor must make “every possible effort to not accept these people back into the country”.



“It’s clear that they have been providing assistance, whether it’s through issuing and distributing passports, whether it’s doing DNA tests,” he said, also pointing to Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke’s relationship with Dr Jamal Rifi, one of the most prominent advocates in the campaign to bring the families home. Labor frontbencher Mark Butler says the IS brides will be met with “the full force of law” at the Australian border. Alex Ellinghausen Burke’s office declined to comment on this story. Taylor questioned why the government had used its powers to block the return of only one member of the cohort. However, the Liberal leader ducked questions on whether he trusted Australia’s security agencies to provide appropriate advice on which people should be blocked. The group would not be the first to be repatriated from Syria.



Related Article Islamic State Australian IS brides make new bid for freedom from Syria The Morrison government brought back eight orphans and one newborn in 2019. In 2022, the Albanese government repatriated four Australian women and their 13 children to Sydney, sparking criticism from political opponents. Dr Rifi, who helped facilitate the group’s first attempt at returning, has previously said Australia would be “safer if the families can return in an orderly fashion to our shores, where the children may receive proper support”. “Children should not suffer the consequences of a parent’s evil deeds,” he wrote at the time. Rifi did not respond to requests for comment.
